source_text: Τοιοῦτον δή τί μοι νόει καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἡλίου. Πλὴν ὅτι ὁ μὲν λαβὼν ἅπαξ καὶ ἐγκεκραμένον ἑαυτῷ τὸ φῶς ἔχων, οὐκ ἀποτίθεται· ἡ δὲ συνεχῶς οἷον ἀποδυομένη καὶ πάλιν ἐπαμφιαζομένη τὸ φῶς, δι' ἑαυτῆς καὶ τὰ περὶ τοῦ ἡλίου εἰρημένα πιστοῦται. Οὗτοι καὶ διαχωρίζειν ἐτάχθησαν ἀνὰ μέσον τῆς ἡμέρας καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τῆς νυκτός. Ἄνω μὲν γὰρ διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ φωτὸς καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ σκότους· τότε δὲ τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν πρὸς τὸ ἐναντίον ἀπέστησεν, ὥστε ἀμίκτως ἔχειν πρὸς ἄλληλα, καὶ φωτὶ πρὸς σκότος μηδεμίαν εἶναι κοινότητα. Ὃ γὰρ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἐστὶν ἡ σκιὰ, τοῦτο οἴεσθαι χρὴ ἐν νυκτὶ τοῦ σκότους εἶναι τὴν φύσιν. Εἰ γὰρ πᾶσα σκιὰ αὐγῆς τινος διαφαινούσης ἀντικειμένως τῷ φωτὶ ἀπὸ τῶν σωμάτων ἐκπίπτει· καὶ ἕωθεν μὲν πρὸς δυσμὰς τέταται, ἑσπέρας δὲ πρὸς ἀνατολὴν ἀποκλίνει, ἐν δὲ τῇ μεσημβρίᾳ ἀρκτῴα γίνεται· καὶ ἡ νὺξ ἐπὶ τὸ ἐναντίον ταῖς ἀκτῖσιν ὑποχωρεῖ, οὐδὲν ἕτερον οὖσα κατὰ τὴν φύσιν ἢ σκίασμα γῆς. Ὡς γὰρ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ἡ σκιὰ τῷ ἀντιφράσσοντι τὴν αὐγὴν παρυφίσταται, οὕτως ἡ νὺξ σκιαζομένου τοῦ περὶ γῆν ἀέρος συνίστασθαι πέφυκε. Τοῦτο τοίνυν ἐστὶ τὸ εἰρημένον, ὅτι Διεχώρισεν ὁ Θεὸς ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ φωτὸς καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ σκότους· ἐπειδὴ τὸ σκότος ὑποφεύγει τοῦ φωτὸς τὰς ἐπιδρομὰς, ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ δημιουργίᾳ φυσικῆς αὐτοῖς τῆς ἀλλοτριώσεως κατασκευασθείσης πρὸς ἄλληλα. Νῦν δὲ ἥλιον ἐπέταξε τοῖς μέτροις τῆς ἡμέρας· καὶ σελήνην, ὅταν ποτὲ πρὸς τὸν ἴδιον κύκλον ἀπαρτισθῇ, ἀρχηγὸν ἐποίησε τῆς νυκτός. Σχεδὸν γὰρ τότε κατὰ διάμετρον οἱ φωστῆρες ἀλλήλοις ἀντικαθίστανται. Ἀνατέλλοντος μὲν γὰρ τοῦ ἡλίου, ἐν ταῖς πανσελήνοις καταφέρεται πρὸς τὸ ἀφανὲς ἡ σελήνη· δυομένου δὲ πάλιν τοῦ ἡλίου, αὕτη πολλάκις ἐξ ἀνατολῶν ἀντανίσχει. Εἰ δὲ κατὰ τὰ ἄλλα σχήματα οὐ συναπαρτίζεται τῇ νυκτὶ τὸ σεληναῖον φῶς, οὐδὲν πρὸς τὸν προκείμενον λόγον. Πλὴν ὅτι ὅταν ἑαυτῆς τελειοτάτη τυγχάνῃ, κατάρχει μὲν τῆς νυκτὸς τῷ ἰδίῳ φωτὶ τὰ ἄστρα ὑπεραυγάζουσα καὶ τὴν γῆν περιλάμπουσα· ἐξίσου δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον τοῦ χρόνου διαιρεῖται τὰ μέτρα. 6.4 Καὶ ἔστωσαν εἰς σημεῖα, καὶ εἰς καιροὺς, καὶ εἰς ἡμέρας, καὶ εἰς ἐνιαυτούς. Ἀναγκαῖαι πρὸς τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον αἱ ἀπὸ τῶν φωστήρων σημειώσεις. Ἐὰν μή τις πέρα τοῦ μέτρου τὰ ἀπ' αὐτῶν σημεῖα περιεργάζηται, χρησίμους αὐτῶν τὰς ἐκ τῆς μακρᾶς ἐμπειρίας παρατηρήσεις εὑρήσει. Πολλὰ μὲν γὰρ περὶ ἐπομβρίας ἐστὶ μαθεῖν· πολλὰ δὲ πε ρὶ αὐχμῶν καὶ πνευμάτων κινήσεως, ἢ μερικῶν ἢ καθόλου, βιαίων ἢ ἀνειμένων. Ἓν γάρ τι τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου παρα δεικνυμένων καὶ ὁ Κύριος ἡμῖν παραδέδωκεν εἰπὼν, ὅτι Χειμὼν ἔσται, στυγνάζει γὰρ πυρράζων ὁ οὐρανός. Ἐπειδὰν γὰρ δι' ἀχλύος ἡ ἀναφορὰ γένηται τοῦ ἡλίου, ἀμαυροῦνται μὲν αἱ ἀκτῖνες, ἀνθρακώδης δὲ καὶ ὕφαιμος τὴν χρόαν ὁρᾶ ται, τῆς παχύτητος τοῦ ἀέρος ταύτην ἐμποιούσης τὴν φαντασίαν ταῖς ὄψεσι. Μὴ διαχεθεὶς δὲ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀκτῖνος ὁ πεπυκνωμένος τέως καὶ συνεστὼς ἀὴρ δῆλός ἐστι διὰ τὴν ἐπίρροιαν τῶν ἐκ τῆς γῆς ἀτμῶν κρατηθῆναι μὴ δυνηθεὶς, ἀλλὰ τῷ πλεονασμῷ τοῦ ὑγροῦ χειμῶνα ἐπάξων τοῖς χωρίοις περὶ ἃ συναθροίζεται.
thought_title: Sun and moon as signs and the nature of night
orientation: Basil is explaining the fourth day's creation of the sun and moon, arguing that night is simply the earth's shadow and that the lights were appointed to mark times and give signs for human life.
pass_a_gloss: Think of something of this kind also in the case of the sun. Except that the one, having received once and having the light mixed with itself, does not put it away; but the other, as it were continually stripping off and again putting on the light, through itself also confirms the things said about the sun. These also were ordered to separate between the day and between the night. For above God separated between the light and between the darkness; but then he set their nature apart toward the opposite, so that they have no mixing with each other, and there is no commonality between light and darkness. For what the shadow is in the day, this one must think the nature of darkness is in the night. For if every shadow of some shining ray, opposing the light, falls from bodies; and in the morning it stretches toward the west, and in the evening it inclines toward the east, and at midday it becomes northern; and the night withdraws to the opposite of the rays, being nothing other in nature than a shadowing of the earth. For as in the day the shadow comes into being alongside that which blocks the ray, so the night naturally comes into being when the air around the earth is shadowed. This therefore is what was said, that God separated between the light and between the darkness; since the darkness flees the onsets of the light, their estrangement from each other having been established as natural in the first creation. But now he appointed the sun to the measures of the day; and the moon, whenever it is completed to its own cycle, he made the ruler of the night. For then the lights stand opposite each other nearly at the diameter. For when the sun rises, at the full moons the moon is carried down toward the unseen; and when the sun sets again, this one often rises opposite from the east. But if according to the other shapes the lunar light is not completed together with the night, it is nothing to the present argument. Except that whenever it is most complete of itself, it begins the night, outshining the stars with its own light and illuminating the earth around; and it divides the measures of time equally with the sun. 6.4 And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years. The indications from the lights are necessary for human life. Unless someone busies himself beyond measure with the signs from them, he will find their observations from long experience useful. For many things about heavy rain can be learned; and many things about droughts and the movement of winds, whether partial or general, violent or slack. For one of the things shown from the sun the Lord also handed down to us, saying, There will be a storm, for the sky reddens, being gloomy. For whenever the rising of the sun happens through mist, the rays are dimmed, and it is seen as coal-like and blood-like in color, the thickness of the air producing this appearance to the eyes. And the air, being dense and compact, not dispersed by the ray, is clear evidence that it could not be overpowered because of the influx of vapors from the earth, but by the excess of moisture will bring a storm upon the regions around which it gathers.

choices.why: The verb means to clothe oneself again; the moon's light is depicted as a garment it repeatedly removes and re-dons, contrasting with the sun's permanent possession.
The noun denotes the act or result of shadowing; Basil is defining night as the earth's shadow cast into the air, not as an independent substance.

choices.english: he made the ruler of the night
choices.why: ἀρχηγός means leader or ruler; Basil is echoing Genesis 1:16 where the moon is appointed to rule the night, so 'ruler' preserves the biblical sense.
The verb means to meddle or over-investigate; Basil is warning against excessive curiosity about celestial signs, not against all observation.

choices.english: for the sky reddens, being gloomy
choices.why: The two participles describe the sky's appearance: gloomy and reddening. Basil quotes Matthew 16:3, and the rendering keeps the causal force of γὰρ.
rejected: for the sky is gloomy and red
for the heaven is lowering and red

pass_b_english: Think of the sun in the same way, with one difference: the sun received the light once and holds it blended with itself, and never puts it off. The moon, by contrast, is continually stripping off the light, so to speak, and putting it on again, and by its own behavior it confirms what has been said about the sun. These lights were also appointed to separate between the day and between the night. For above, God separated between the light and between the darkness; then he set their natures in opposition to each other, so that they have no mixing with one another, and light has nothing in common with darkness. What a shadow is in the daytime, that is what we should understand the nature of darkness to be at night. For every shadow falls from bodies that block a shining ray, lying opposite the light; in the morning it stretches toward the west, in the evening it leans toward the east, and at noon it lies to the north. So too the night withdraws in the direction opposite the sun's rays, being nothing other in its nature than a shadowing of the earth. Just as in the daytime a shadow comes into being from whatever blocks the light, so the night naturally comes into being when the air around the earth is cast into shadow. This, then, is what is meant by the words, God separated between the light and between the darkness: the darkness flees the assaults of the light, because at the first creation their estrangement from one another was built into their natures. But now he commanded the sun to govern the measures of the day, and the moon, whenever it completes its own cycle, he made the ruler of the night. For at that time the lights stand nearly opposite one another across the diameter. When the sun rises at the full moon, the moon sinks down out of sight; and when the sun sets again, the moon often rises opposite it from the east. If in its other phases the moon's light does not exactly coincide with the night, that has no bearing on the present discussion. The point is that when the moon is at its fullest, it begins the night, outshining the stars with its own light and illuminating the earth, and it divides the measures of time equally with the sun. "And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years" (Genesis 1:14). The indications given by the lights are necessary for human life. If one does not busy himself beyond measure with the signs they give, he will find their observations, gained from long experience, useful. From them one can learn many things about heavy rain, and many things about droughts and the movement of winds, whether local or general, violent or gentle. One of the signs drawn from the sun the Lord himself has handed on to us, when he said, "There will be a storm, for the sky reddens, being gloomy" (Matthew 16:3). For when the sun rises through mist, its rays are dimmed, and its color appears like coals and tinged with blood, because the thickness of the air produces this appearance to the eyes. The air, which until then was dense and compact and not dispersed by the ray, shows that it could not be overcome because of the influx of vapors from the earth, but by the excess of moisture it will bring a storm upon the regions where it gathers.
